rows.title: Coronavirus And The Gig Economy
rows.standfirst: Many gig workers have suddenly found themselves providing essential services during the COVID-19 pandemic. But many also feel like they have to work in an unsafe situation.

rows.title: Facebook Grants For Coronavirus News Coverage: 3 Questions With Campbell Brown
rows.standfirst: Campbell Brown, Facebook's head of news partnerships, describes the company's $100 million investment in local news agencies.

rows.title: Walmart Faces Lawsuit Over Worker's Death From Coronavirus Complications
rows.standfirst: The wrongful-death case alleges Walmart ignored symptoms and failed to safeguard workers. The legal complaint is by the family of one of two employees from the same store who died in recent weeks.

rows.title: Many Struggling Homeowners Not Getting The Mortgage Relief U.S. Promised
rows.standfirst: Millions of homeowners who've lost their incomes qualify to defer payments. But many say lenders are demanding unfair terms such as massive subsequent lump sum payments that they can't afford.

rows.title: With Survival At Stake, Small Business Owners Frustrated By Aid Delays
rows.standfirst: The Paycheck Protection Program is meant to help small businesses keep workers on payroll. But first, businesses have to get the money — a process that has proven difficult for some.

rows.title: Honda, Nissan Furlough Workers As Auto Plant Shutdowns Are Extended
rows.standfirst: Auto assembly plants across the country continue to be closed amid the coronavirus pandemic. Tens of thousands of workers are going without pay.

rows.title: Meat Processing Plants Suspend Operations After Workers Fall Ill
rows.standfirst: Several processing plants in the U.S. are sitting idle this week because workers are sick with the coronavirus. Other facilities are still operating, but fewer workers are showing up.

rows.title: More Aid Coming For Small Businesses, Senate Majority Leader McConnell Says
rows.standfirst: The $350 billion small business program created in the massive coronavirus relief package is popular, and multiple senators say more money is needed to keep it afloat.

rows.title: Jamie Dimon Warns 'A Bad Recession' Is Coming
rows.standfirst: In a letter to shareholders, the JPMorgan Chase CEO applauds the government and the Fed for quick work, but says the pandemic will have devastating consequences for the global economy.

rows.title: 4 Of 5 Workers Are Affected By COVID-19 Worldwide, U.N. Agency Says
rows.standfirst: The COVID-19 pandemic is taking a terrible toll on the world's economy, with lockdown measures now affecting the livelihood of almost 2.7 billion workers, according to a new report.

rows.title: States, Hospitals Say They're Still Not Getting Vital Supplies To Fight COVID-19
rows.standfirst: President Trump says the government's procurement and distribution system is "a fine-tuned machine," but many hospitals and state governors say they're struggling to get what they need.

rows.title: Are We Firing Too Many People In The U.S.?
rows.standfirst: Instead of mass layoffs, Germany tries to safeguard employment. Under a program called Kurzarbeit , when companies declare they're under financial distress, the government helps pay their workers.

rows.title: Airline Flights Into And Out Of New York City Cut Drastically Because Of Coronavirus
rows.standfirst: A spokesperson said American Airline's busiest flight out of LaGuardia Sunday only had 27 passengers and nine flights from JFK and LaGuardia had one passenger on each.

rows.title: Starbucks Now Requires Employees To Wear Face Coverings At Work
rows.standfirst: Starting Tuesday, employees must wear face coverings. Those who don't have their own, the company created a tutorial on how to make one using store supplies.

rows.title: Pandemic-onomics: Lessons From The Spanish Flu
rows.standfirst: Different cities responded in different ways to the Spanish Flu outbreak of 1918. And their economies fared differently as a result.

rows.title: Rural Hospitals: The Waiting Game
rows.standfirst: Rural hospitals already walk a scalpel's edge between solvency and collapse. Coronavirus threatens to push many of them over the brink.

rows.title: Airlines Reach Agreement With Treasury Department On Share Of Coronavirus Aid
rows.standfirst: To prevent mass layoffs of airline employees, Congress authorized $50 billion in grants and loans for the carriers, as part of the $2.3 trillion economic relief package approved last month.

rows.title: Amid Historic Oil Bust, Texas Debates The Once Unthinkable: Keep It In The Ground
rows.standfirst: Texas regulators have not capped production since 1973, but some smaller producers want such a move to try and stave off bankruptcy. Oil demand and prices have crashed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

rows.title: Instagram Rival Cuts A Third Of Staff As Market Changes 'Overnight'
rows.standfirst: VSCO is one of more than 200 technology startups that have laid off employees in the economic tumult caused by the coronavirus.

rows.title: Grocery Workers Should Be Designated First Responders, Supermarkets And Union Say
rows.standfirst: Kroger and Albertsons have joined the food workers union UFCW in urging state and national officials to give grocery staff higher priority for testing and access to masks and other protections.

rows.title: How One City Mayor Forced A Pork Giant To Close Its Virus-Stricken Plant
rows.standfirst: Smithfield Foods didn't want to stop slaughtering hogs at its Sioux Falls pork plant, even after hundreds of workers got sick with the coronavirus. Then the city's mayor forced the company's hand.

rows.title: Getting Back To Normal: Big Tech's Solution Depends On Public Trust
rows.standfirst: Apple and Google are developing a tool that relies on Bluetooth signals, sent by smartphones, to let people know if they may have been exposed to the coronavirus.

rows.title: U.N. Chief Targets 'Dangerous Epidemic Of Misinformation' On Coronavirus
rows.standfirst: "Harmful health advice and snake-oil solutions are proliferating," U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said. "Wild conspiracy theories are infecting the Internet. Hatred is going viral."

rows.title: Florida Designates Pro Wrestling 'Essential Business'
rows.standfirst: Florida's statewide stay-at-home order no longer applies to pro wrestling. Governor Ron DeSantis made the change and WWE resumed its live television shows on Monday without fans in attendance.

rows.title: IMF Warns Of Steepest Recession Since The Great Depression
rows.standfirst: The fallout from the coronavirus will be much worse than that of the financial crisis, the IMF says. The global economy is expected to shrink by 3% this year; the U.S. GDP could fall twice as much.

rows.title: Coronavirus-Stricken Cities Have Empty Hospitals, But Reopening Them Is Difficult
rows.standfirst: In Philadelphia, New Orleans and Los Angeles, former safety-net hospitals sit empty. But reopening a closed hospital, even when demand for health resources spikes, is not easy or cheap.

rows.title: America's Largest Bank, JPMorgan Chase, Prepares For A Massive Round Of Defaults
rows.standfirst: JPMorgan Chase set aside the largest amount of money since 2010 to prepare for defaults, as its profit fell 69%. Wells Fargo's earnings sank 89%.

rows.title: Unicorn Riding Scooter In Fatal Crash
rows.standfirst: As venture capital retreats, hot startups are collapsing.

rows.title: Bloomberg News Killed Investigation, Fired Reporter, Then Sought To Silence His Wife
rows.standfirst: The investigation into Chinese political elites would "wipe out everything we've tried to build there," Matthew Winkler, Bloomberg's editor-in-chief at the time, said on audiotape obtained by NPR.

rows.title: States Unite On Reopening Economies: 'Science — Not Politics — Will Guide' Decisions
rows.standfirst: "Any plan to reopen society MUST be driven by data and experts," said Gov. Andrew Cuomo of New York, which is forming a regional coalition of states. California will work with Oregon and Washington.

rows.title: Chamber Of Commerce Head Welcomes New Coronavirus Bill, Gradual Reopening Of Economy
rows.standfirst: Suzanne Clark, president of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, tells All Things Considered that reopening the economy "will be phased in." She also says businesses will need more help to survive.

rows.title: Oil: Less Than Zero
rows.standfirst: The price of a barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude oil fell below zero. In other words, suppliers were paying people to take it off their hands. How did that happen? And what does it mean?

rows.title: Data Of Nearly 8,000 Small Businesses May Have Been Exposed, SBA Says
rows.standfirst: "Personal identifiable information" was potentially exposed to other businesses via an online lending application portal, a spokesperson for the Small Business Administration told NPR.

rows.title: Amazon Workers Stage New Protests Over Warehouse Coronavirus Safety
rows.standfirst: Organizers say more than 350 workers pledged to call off work, criticizing Amazon's measures to protect them during the coronavirus pandemic. Amazon says it has taken steps to keep workers safe.

rows.title: Some Not-So-Small Companies Are Getting Small-Business Loans Under PPP
rows.standfirst: The government's $349 billion Paycheck Protection Program had to be thrown together quickly, and the criteria for which companies can receive benefits were kept loose.

rows.title: Airlines Offer Vouchers, Credits For Canceled Flights. Customers Want Cash
rows.standfirst: A new survey suggests nearly 60 million Americans are losing money because of canceled plans. And would-be travelers are getting the runaround, even when they are legally entitled to a full refund.

rows.title: Record Oil Price Drops Send Stock Markets Diving, Too
rows.standfirst: The Dow fell 631 points a day after oil prices turned negative for the first time ever. The drops are the latest market reactions to the global economic downturn caused by the pandemic.

rows.title: Why Is The Fed Sending Billions Of Dollars All Over The World?
rows.standfirst: As COVID-19 causes a global meltdown, the world turns to the U.S. Federal Reserve.

rows.title: Study Raises Questions About False Negatives From Quick COVID-19 Test
rows.standfirst: New research suggests the Abbott ID NOW test, which produces results in less than 15 minutes, is the most likely among common tests to reassure people they are not infected when they really are.

rows.title: Bitter Taste For Coffee Shop Owner, As New $600 Jobless Benefit Drove Her To Close
rows.standfirst: The new federal benefit is designed to cushion the blow of the pandemic. But some businesses that want to stay open say it's hard to do so when employees can make more money by staying home.

rows.title: Company With Ties To Trump Receives Millions From Small Business Loan Program
rows.standfirst: Many businesses have struggled to get any money from the Paycheck Protection Program. But a company owned by a prominent Chicago family received a $5.5 million loan.

rows.title: Georgia Beginning To Reopen Its Economy, Lifting Some Coronavirus-Crisis Limits
rows.standfirst: Gov. Brian Kemp cited favorable data and more testing in his decision to reopen businesses such as gyms, tattoo parlors and hair salons this Friday. Pennsylvania and Tennessee also announced changes.

rows.title: Coronavirus And The Digital Divide
rows.standfirst: We're spending more time at home, and more time with technology — highlighting a deep digital divide in the United States and introducing thorny ethical dilemmas.

rows.title: This Charmin Factory Keeps Humming Even As Much Of America Is Hunkered Down
rows.standfirst: Although millions of Americans are out of work or working from home, many are still working at factories nationwide. They have some lessons on what it will take to "reopen" the country safely.

rows.title: Can Colleges Survive Coronavirus? 'The Math Is Not Pretty'
rows.standfirst: Colleges around the U.S. moved classes online during the pandemic. Some are considering keeping their campuses shut in the fall — which means hiring freezes, smaller admissions and even layoffs.

rows.title: Passengers Must Wear Masks On Major Airlines To Cut Spread Of Coronavirus
rows.standfirst: Southwest, Alaska, American, Delta and United Airlines are joining JetBlue and Frontier in requiring face coverings amid growing pressure from Congress and their own employees.

rows.title: Essential Workers
rows.standfirst: Essential workers put themselves at risk of infection every day to keep the economy running. But many aren't well protected or compensated for the dangerous work they do.

rows.title: American Airlines And United Report Nearly $4 Billion In Combined Losses
rows.standfirst: Few industries have been as hard hit by the pandemic as airlines, as the number of air travelers has plummeted.

rows.title: A Staggering Toll: 30 Million Have Filed For Unemployment
rows.standfirst: Another 3.8 million people filed claims for unemployment last week, as the coronavirus pandemic continues to weigh on the U.S. job market. That brought the total for the past 6 weeks to 30.3 million.

rows.title: Buybacks And Bailouts
rows.standfirst: Over the past decade, American companies spent billions buying back their own shares. Now they need a taxpayer rescue. Do they deserve it? | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Tesla's Elon Musk Rants Again, Calls Lockdowns Forcible Imprisonment And 'Fascist'
rows.standfirst: Tesla's CEO downplayed the virus last month, tweeting on March 19 that based on the trends at the time, there would "probably" be "close to zero new cases" in the United States "by end of April."

rows.title: Workers Scared As Trump Orders Meat Plants To Open During Coronavirus Crisis
rows.standfirst: The president invoked the Defense Production Act after more than a dozen beef, pork and poultry plants across the country shut down either temporarily or indefinitely in the past few weeks.

rows.title: NFL Commissioner Gives Up His $40 Million Salary And Will Cut League Employees' Pay
rows.standfirst: The news of Roger Goodell's pay cut came as an internal league memo announced executive salary reductions and furloughs of league employees. He said coronavirus-control disruptions are to blame.

rows.title: Getting Back To Business
rows.standfirst: Small and medium size enterprises tend not to have much of a cash cushion, so most are desperate to get back to work. But many are finding that reopening after a pandemic is a messy business.

rows.title: Grocery Cashier Is 'Putting A Little Positivity' Into Seniors' Shopping Trips
rows.standfirst: Grocery stores have carved out special shopping times for seniors and others. "Just to be able to spend that one-on-one time with ... them. They definitely make me laugh," Courtney Meadows says.

rows.title: Boeing Cuts Its Workforce Due To The Coronavirus Crisis
rows.standfirst: The airplane manufacturer said it will eliminate nearly 16,000 jobs. Airlines are on pace to lose about $300 billion this year and aren't likely to be buying planes anytime soon.

rows.title: Scram Big Banks: Small Lenders Take Over SBA Lending Program (For A Night)
rows.standfirst: The SBA chief announced that only small banks will be given access to the Payroll Protection Program for eight hours, after heavy criticism that the program had given money to well-known businesses.

rows.title: Lyft Lays Off Nearly 1,000 Employees As Virus Saps Demand For Rides
rows.standfirst: The ride-hailing company is also furloughing hundreds of workers and cutting pay as it tries to reduce costs during the coronavirus pandemic.

rows.title: Italy Considers Permits For Undocumented Migrants To Fill A Big Farmworker Gap
rows.standfirst: The country faces a shortfall of up to 350,000 laborers just when it is bracing for deep economic impacts from the novel coronavirus pandemic.

rows.title: Colorado City Employee Donates Stimulus Check To 3 Local Charities
rows.standfirst: Scott Severs and his wife Julie Bartlett have been able to pay their mortgage and they have a healthy emergency fund. So he donated his federal rescue check, though he acknowledges not everyone can.
